clue.text: Raises false alarm as crow flies not straight

indicators.note: a path that is not straight is crooked, so the letters of crow flies are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone sounds an alarm because a bird's flight path wanders, inverting the phrase 'as the crow flies'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as crow flies' looks like the familiar idiom for a straight line; 'not straight' undoes it by scrambling CROWFLIES.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from Aesop's shepherd boy, who repeatedly gave false warnings of a predator until nobody believed him.

clue.text: College is down in seaside town

parts.note: someone who is down (out of pocket) owes money

explanation.surface: A student is feeling low while staying at a resort by the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is down' reads as being sad, but here it means being in debt.
explanation.definitionFit: Cowes is a sailing resort on the Isle of Wight, off England's south coast, home of an annual regatta.

clue.text: Not-so-wise guy stupidly smug on air

indicators.note: doing something stupidly means doing it in a muddled way, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A dim fellow is broadcasting with an air of self-satisfaction.
explanation.definitionFit: A know-nothing, an ignorant person, is the opposite of a wise guy, hence the playful 'not-so-wise'.

clue.text: Explorer's hut split

definitions.note: read as 'Explorer is', the definition being the explorer and the 's a link

parts.note: a shack is a rough hut
to split, in slang, is to blab or reveal a secret, to let on

explanation.surface: A polar explorer's hut has cracked open.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a possessive: Shackleton's preserved Antarctic huts are famous. In the cryptic reading the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Ernest Shackleton was the Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer who led the Endurance expedition.

clue.text: Writer opens Milton's text, not the first volume

indicators.note: the writer goes into the next piece, as if opening it up from inside
says the opening letter of the text's title is dropped

parts.note: Comus is a masque by John Milton
a nib is the writing point of a pen, a classic crossword writer

explanation.surface: An author starts reading Milton's work, though not the opening volume.
explanation.walkthrough: Comus is a 1634 masque by John Milton, not his best-known work; 'Writer' as a pen's nib is a standard crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: An omnibus is a single large volume collecting several works, such as a novelist's trilogy.

clue.text: Little animal picked up by police, showing limp

indicators.note: in a down answer, something picked up is lifted so it reads from bottom to top, i.e. backwards

parts.note: a calf is a young cow, a little animal
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of British police forces

explanation.surface: Officers collect a small creature that seems lame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' works as a reversal only because this is a down entry, read upwards. CID is Britain's plain-clothes detective branch.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something lacking firmness or stiffness, hanging loose like a wilted plant.

clue.text: Revolting dog I would turn out of the ground

indicators.note: revolting means turning over, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: a pug is a small breed of dog
I'd is the contraction of I would

explanation.surface: A disgusting dog is going to be dug up from the earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' poses as disgusting but signals turning PUGID backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To unearth something is to excavate it, bringing it up out of the soil.

clue.text: Toy poodle has left Lima for good

indicators.note: one thing put in for another replaces it; here two letters stand in place of the one

parts.note: a poodle is a breed of dog
Lima is L in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A miniature poodle has quit Peru's capital permanently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lima' looks like the city and 'for good' like 'permanently'; instead L and L replace G in DOG.
explanation.definitionFit: A doll is a child's plaything shaped like a person, a classic example of a toy.

clue.text: Upset stomach on a grand scale

indicators.note: in a down answer, set up means turned upward, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: tum is an informal word for stomach
G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: A queasy stomach on a grand scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' poses as queasy but reverses TUMAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamut is a full range, originally the whole series of musical notes, so a scale.

clue.text: Beg God to manage successfully

parts.note: Pan is the Greek god of the wild
to handle something is to cope with it well

explanation.surface: Pray to the Almighty to cope well.
explanation.definitionFit: To panhandle is American slang for asking strangers in the street for money.

clue.text: Not right to cheat American out of money

indicators.note: not having something means going without it, so the following letter is dropped

parts.note: to wrong someone is to treat them unfairly, to cheat them

explanation.surface: It is wrong to swindle an American out of his cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Wonga is British slang for cash, as in 'a load of wonga'.

clue.text: One not quite a success in new Park film

parts.note: Early Man is a 2018 stop-motion film by Nick Park of Aardman Animations

explanation.surface: Someone who fails narrowly appears in a fresh movie from Park.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Park is the creator of Wallace and Gromit.
explanation.definitionFit: A nearly man is someone who repeatedly comes close to winning or achieving something but never does.

clue.text: To perform flogging is to act as the Empire did

definitions.meaning: flogging means hitting someone across the back

definitions.text: to act as the Empire did
definitions.meaning: in the Star Wars sequel title, the Empire retaliates

explanation.surface: A flogging is what the empire did, oddly, as if a colonial power ordered the lash.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both lashing someone across the back and retaliating, as in the film 'The Empire Strikes Back'.

clue.text: At intervals, Neptunian geographical feature that explodes

indicators.note: taking letters at intervals means every other one, here the even-placed letters

explanation.surface: A volcanic feature on Neptune erupts every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: Neptunian also means formed by water, so the surface plays on geology.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the active volcano in Sicily, a mountain that erupts.

clue.text: Highly planned escape route?

parts.note: an aircraft's planned course through the sky, high up, and also a route for flight in the sense of escape

explanation.surface: A carefully organised getaway plan.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft's course is planned in advance at altitude, while flight is also fleeing, so a way out.

clue.text: Gets in the way of extracting copper from gourds

indicators.note: extracting something means pulling it out, so the copper symbol is taken away

parts.note: cucumbers belong to the gourd family
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: Something hampers the mining of copper from squash-like fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: To encumber or hinder someone is to obstruct them, a verb usage now somewhat old-fashioned.

clue.text: Policeman back on duty, yes? It's an act

parts.note: cop is slang for a policeman

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: 'Right?' asks for agreement, like 'yes?'

explanation.surface: An officer returns to his shift and asks whether it is all a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back on duty' looks like returning to work; it means the last letter of 'duty'. The UK statute is the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act.
explanation.definitionFit: Laws protecting authors' work are passed as statutes, commonly called a Copyright Act.

clue.text: Thrown off toboggan and soaked?

parts.note: being thrown off a luge, a racing toboggan, could jokingly be called being ..., and a downpour also drenches you

explanation.surface: A sledger tipped off into the snow and got wet.
explanation.definitionFit: Deluged means flooded or drenched with water, as by a downpour.

clue.text: No force in camouflage sported something of avocado

indicators.note: sported in the sense of played around with, so the letters are rearranged
with no force means the force letter is left out

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for force in physics

explanation.surface: Without force, camouflage was worn by a dish of avocado.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove F from CAMOUFLAGE, then 'sported' rearranges CAMOULAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Guacamole is the Mexican dip made of mashed avocado.

clue.text: Exeat for graduate

definitions.meaning: an exeat is a permit to leave school or college for a time, a leave slip
to complete a training course, especially military

explanation.definitionFit: A pass to go out of a boarding school is an exeat, and cadets finishing training at a military academy pass out.

clue.text: Clear intent to obtain weapon

indicators.note: the tent obtains, or takes in, the other piece, so it goes inside

parts.note: split as 'in tent', the camping shelter, with in confirming the containment
to clear something of a nuisance is to rid it

explanation.surface: Someone has a clear plan to get hold of a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is to read 'intent' as 'in tent': RID in TENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A trident is a three-pronged spear, the weapon of Neptune and of Roman gladiators.

clue.text: What one Greek moving into China does?

definitions.text: What one Greek moving into China does?

indicators.note: something moving into a place goes inside it

parts.note: in Cockney rhyming slang, china plate means mate
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A Greek relocating to China is doing what emigrants do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is Cockney rhyming slang (china plate = mate), not the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone relocating from one country to another is moving their home, which birds and people do when they change region.

clue.text: Detective resolves 19 across

indicators.note: resolving something breaks it down into parts, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: refers to the answer of the across clue numbered 19

explanation.surface: A sleuth cracks a case involving the other clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolves' looks like what a detective does to a case; it rearranges the letters of 19 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Maigret is Georges Simenon's fictional Parisian police inspector.

clue.text: We hear Big Bird to be highly enjoyable

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, signalling that the word sounds like another

parts.note: the roc is a giant mythical bird of Arabian legend

explanation.surface: Apparently the Sesame Street character is great fun.
explanation.walkthrough: Big Bird is the Sesame Street character; here it is the roc, the enormous bird of the Arabian Nights.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, something that is great or excellent is said to be awesome, as in 'this band really is great'.

clue.text: Flower, roughly every one coming up

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means roughly or approximately

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means read from the bottom, i.e. backwards

parts.note: all means every one

explanation.surface: A flower emerges more or less everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The calla is an arum lily, a plant grown for its white trumpet-shaped spathe.

clue.text: Attendant sprinted short way ahead to junction

indicators.note: ahead tells us the short way comes before the running in the answer

parts.note: mini means small or short, as in miniskirt
St is the abbreviation for street, a way
ran is the past tense of run, so sprinted
a T-junction gives the letter T

explanation.surface: A servant raced a brief distance to reach a crossroads.
explanation.definitionFit: A ministrant is one who ministers or serves, especially an assistant at a church service.

clue.text: Water gets into dry post

indicators.note: one piece getting into another is placed inside it

parts.note: TT means teetotal, i.e. dry
wee is informal for urine, making water

explanation.surface: Moisture seeps into a fence post that should be dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water' is urine (to make water), and 'post' is a message on social media.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweet is a short message posted on Twitter, now X.

clue.text: Roughly cut fuel at hospital

parts.note: gas is a fuel
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A wound cut carelessly is treated with gas at the hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: A gash is a long deep wound, the kind of jagged slit left by a ragged blade.

clue.text: Large ideogram represented former PM

indicators.note: represented means presented again, so the letters are put in a fresh arrangement

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A big pictorial character stood for an ex-premier.
explanation.definitionFit: Golda Meir was prime minister of Israel from 1969 to 1974.

clue.text: A beautiful original poem, Home

indicators.note: the original part of a word is its origin, its first letter

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: A lovely, novel poem titled 'Home'.
explanation.definitionFit: An abode is a dwelling place, a formal word for a residence.

clue.text: Scraps expert conclusion? Unwise

indicators.note: a word's conclusion is its final letter

parts.note: rash means hasty and unwise

explanation.surface: A specialist decides to discard things, but the decision is ill-judged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scraps' reads as a verb but the definition is the noun: leftover rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Scraps are worthless leftovers, i.e. rubbish or garbage.

clue.text: Very short time, most irritating

parts.note: itchiest is the superlative of itchy, so most irritating

explanation.surface: A brief moment that is extremely annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very short' is the superlative: titchy is British slang for tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Titchy is British informal for tiny, from Little Tich the music-hall comedian, so this is the smallest of all.
